gradual

/GRAD-oo-ul/ — emphasis on first syllable · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Gradual means happening slowly and in small stages rather than all at once.

No flood or earthquake shaped these towering walls; instead, the change was gradual, so slow that no single generation would ever have noticed it.

Example

The patient stopped smoking, and her lung capacity improved month by month—slowly at first, then more noticeably—a gradual recovery that her doctor marked on a chart.

Gradual is more precise than a plain word like 'slow' or 'better' because it emphasizes that the change happens in distinct stages over time, not just slowly.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

slow: Slow describes an unhurried pace and nothing more. Gradual adds structure to the slowness: a gradual change unfolds in small stages, each building on the last. A slow train is merely unhurried; a gradual recovery happens step by noticeable step.

progressive: Progressive means advancing step by step, each stage carrying the process further — a progressive illness moves stage to stage; a progressive tax rises bracket by bracket. Gradual describes only the slow pace of change: progress can be brisk and still progressive, but never brisk and gradual.

steady: Steady means regular and even — holding the same rate or state without change. Gradual is about slow movement through stages, so a gradual thing is always changing, just slowly. A steady hum never varies at all; a gradual thaw is different every day.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

sudden: happening all at once, without warning

instantaneous: finished completely in a single instant

Where it sits · how slow the pace is

gradual → sluggish → glacial

sluggish vs. gradual: Traffic on the flooded highway was sluggish, dragging along at a barely moving crawl; gradual is gentler, describing change that is slow but keeps making steady, staged progress toward somewhere.

glacial vs. gradual: Progress on the trade treaty was glacial, so slow that it felt like nothing was moving at all; gradual is the better word for the reservoir's rise behind the new dam, because it promises real, measurable advancement in stages rather than mere extreme slowness.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — gradu-: step, degree (Latin gradus, 'a step' — the u comes along from gradus itself)

Suffix — -al: relating to, of the nature of

Put it together: Gradu- (step, degree — straight from Latin gradus, 'a step,' keeping its u) + -al (relating to) = relating to steps or degrees — happening one small step at a time rather than all at once. There is no prefix hiding here. The same stepping root walks through grade, graduate, and upgrade.

Use the root in a new word: upgrade: The airline decided to upgrade the passengers sitting in coach to first-class seats.

Word Choice

neutral

Gradual describes change that's slow and happens in stages—perfect when you want to show that something advances in noticeable increments. When the slowness matters more than the stages, 'slow' alone is fine.
